**The Weight of Silence and the Whisper of Stars**

There is a quiet hum beneath the surface of everything—an unspoken rhythm that pulses through the air, the earth, the very bones of the world. It is the silence between words, the pause before a storm, the stillness before a breath is taken. We often mistake this silence for emptiness, but it is not empty. It is full—full of possibility, of memory, of the weight of all that has been and all that could be. And yet, we fear it. We fill it with noise, with chatter, with the endless scroll of screens and the clatter of keys, as if the silence might swallow us whole.

I have spent a lot of time in silence lately. Not the silence of a library or a meditation cushion, but the deeper, gnawing silence that comes when the world feels too loud, too heavy, too full of things that don’t belong to you. It is the silence that lingers after a conversation ends, the one that sits in the back of your throat when you know you should say something but don’t. It is the silence of a room where no one is quite sure what to do with themselves, where the air is thick with the unspoken.

I think about silence often because I think about time. Time is silence, too—long stretches of it where nothing happens, where the clock ticks on and nothing changes. And yet, in those moments, something always does. A seed sprouts. A thought takes root. A heart learns to beat differently.

I was thinking about this the other day as I stood on a hill at dusk, watching the sky bleed into purple and gold. The wind carried the scent of damp earth and wildflowers, and for a moment, everything was still. No cars. No voices. No alarms. Just the slow, deliberate breath of the world. And in that stillness, I felt something shift inside me. Not a revelation, not a grand truth, but a quiet understanding—that the world is not just noise and movement, that there is space between the beats of the heart, and that space is where meaning lives.

I wonder if we forget this. If we are so busy rushing, so consumed by the next thing, the next distraction, that we lose touch with the quiet. The poets and the philosophers have always known this. They have written about it in verses and essays, in paintings and songs. They have called it *sabbatical*, *contemplation*, *the space between thoughts*. But in our modern world, where everything is immediate and everything is for sale, these ideas feel like relics. Like something from another time.

And yet, I think they are more necessary than ever.

Because here is the thing about silence: it is not the absence of sound. It is the presence of something deeper. It is the space where the soul can breathe. Where the mind can wander without judgment. Where the heart can remember what it is to be soft.

I have been trying to listen to the silence more. Not just the silence of the world, but the silence within myself. The silence that comes when you close your eyes and let your thoughts drift, when you stop trying to control the narrative of your own life. It is a dangerous thing, this silence. It is where the truth lives. And the truth is not always pretty.

I think about the people I love—the ones who are here, and the ones who are not. I think about the mistakes I have made, the regrets, the moments I wish I could unlive. And in the silence, they are all there, like ghosts in the static. But they are not just ghosts. They are echoes. They are the things that have shaped me, that have made me who I am. And in the silence, I can hear them. Not as complaints, not as judgments, but as part of the song.

I have been reading a lot of old books lately. Books that were written when people still believed in the power of silence, in the idea that there was meaning to be found in stillness. Books like *The Book of the City of Ladies* by Christine de Pizan, where a woman argues with her doubts and fears, and finds strength in the silence of her own mind. Or *Walden* by Henry David Thoreau, where he writes about living simply, about the beauty of the natural world, and the necessity of solitude. These books are not just historical artifacts. They are maps. They show us how to navigate the silence, how to find our way when the world feels overwhelming.

I have also been thinking about the stars. Not just the stars as they appear in the sky, but the stars as metaphors—the distant, twinkling lights that remind us of how small we are, and how vast the universe is. The stars are silent. They do not speak. They do not demand anything of us. They simply are. And yet, they have shaped our lives in ways we cannot even imagine. They have guided sailors across oceans, inspired poets to write, and given us a sense of wonder that nothing else can.

I wonder if we could learn from the stars. If we could learn to be as silent as they are, as unassuming, as patient. If we could trust that our light, too, will find its way, even if we cannot see it yet.

I have been trying to do this. To be more like the stars. To let go of the need to explain myself, to justify my existence, to fill every moment with noise. Instead, I am trying to sit with the silence. To let it hold me. To let it remind me that I am not alone, even when I feel like I am.

And sometimes, in the silence, I hear things. Not words, not exactly. But a kind of hum. A vibration. A sense of connection that transcends language. It is the hum of the world, the hum of the universe, the hum of all the things that have ever been and all the things that will be. And in that hum, I feel less alone. I feel less afraid.

I think about the future, too. About the world that is coming, and the world that is leaving. I think about the children who will grow up in a world that is different from mine, in ways I cannot yet imagine. And I wonder what kind of silence they will know. Will they know the silence of the stars? Or will they know only the noise of their own devices, the constant hum of the internet, the endless chatter of social media?

I hope they know both. I hope they know how to listen to the silence, and how to make their own noise when it is needed. I hope they know that silence is not the absence of something, but the presence of everything.

Because here is the truth: the world is full. Full of sound and silence, of light and dark, of life and death. And in all of that fullness, there is space. There is always space. And in that space, we can find ourselves.

So I will keep listening to the silence. I will keep looking at the stars. And I will keep trying to remember what it means to be quiet, to be still, to be present. Because in the end, that is all we really have. The present moment. The silence between the beats of our hearts. The stars above us, twinkling in the dark.

And if we listen closely, we might just hear the world answering back.
